rulings.ruling: B, professional-calm, for every product surface (root README, in-app UI text, error and empty states, the install/first-run path, USER_WALKTHROUGH_GUIDE); A, peer-expert, for docs/ technical references, docs/adr/, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and REPO_GUIDE. A material is linked, never blended in place. C is not taken on any surface family.
rulings.note: The operator's audience answer is "both, equally" and both halves are technical (people who already installed a Hermes agent, plus himself), so the mixed-audience clause fires; with no money, no regulated data and no consumer anywhere in the venture, the C trigger never does.
rulings.conflict:
Four contradictions with what PatterStage does today, the first being the serious one.

1. THE GATE ENFORCES THE VOICE LAW ON EXACTLY THE WRONG REGISTER. scripts/tooling/design-lint.mjs:138 scopes no-em-dash to `files: (f) => f.startsWith("docs/") && f.endsWith(".md")`. Under this ruling docs/ is the A surface, the one a peer reads and the one that needs the law least. The B surfaces are all outside it: root README.md (13 em-dashes), AGENTS.md (4) and CLAUDE.md (4) fall outside SCAN_DIRS = ["src","docs"] entirely, and src/ is walked but exempted by the predicate, carrying em-dashes on 1,518 lines across 532 ts/tsx files including shipped copy (orchestration/chat subtitle "Talk to your Hermes agent - tools, memory, live runs"; sessions empty state; laboratory/artifacts subtitle; config/seed "Drift - disk differs from database"). The voice module's own activation triggers name "UI text" and "error messages" first. So the only mechanically enforced voice rule in this repo protects the surfaces a stranger never reads and leaves untouched the ones that decide whether they stay.

2. VOICE LAW RULE 4 IS VIOLATED LIVE AND UNGATED IN THE UI: "Saved!" (src/app/config/[section]/page.tsx:256, src/app/operations/agents/page.tsx:578), "Copied!" (operations/personalities/page.tsx:107), "Personality saved!" (:319), "Your story is ready!" (modules/rec-room/components/GenerateOverlay.tsx:89). No rule catches these.

3. THE README IS NOT IN B. It opens on a slogan ("The Stage is _Yours._") and bolds nearly every noun phrase in its feature table. B states facts and shows records rather than making claims; that page makes claims. It is also the single highest-traffic surface for death #1 and is the one file with no voice gate on it at all.

4. USER_WALKTHROUGH_GUIDE.md DECLARES ITS OWN UNRULED REGISTER at line 5 ("written for the Junior developer / operator"), a scaffolded fourth register nobody chose, and carries 158 em-dashes, the largest single entry in the 869-violation baseline. Under this ruling it is a B product surface.

Separately, the doctrine's banned-list pattern requires every venture to keep one and PatterStage has none anywhere in the repo. The seed list is effectively clean in prose already (all 11 `unlock` hits are achievement-progression identifiers, `elevate` is "elevated PowerShell"), so the list is cheap to write; the missing part is the check.

One thing I declined to rule and want on the record: it is tempting to take C on the install path because death #1 is "clone-and-run is too high a bar". I did not, because the brief names that death's mechanism as packaging ("the .exe never ships"), not register. Warm-guide copy does not ship an installer, and ruling C there would let a copy edit stand in for the fix. Related finding, outside this batch: src/ has no onboarding, welcome or first-run surface at all (find for onboard/setup/welcome/first-run under src returns nothing), so the first-run surface family this ruling governs does not yet exist in the app.

rulings.ruling: C (the tree is the architecture, over the machine contract)
rulings.note: src/modules/ plus the three named composition points already make a file's location answer "may I import this", and design-lint runs the contract inside npm run lint and CI.
rulings.conflict: PatterStage took C without the canary the rule requires: tests/ contains no snapshot, golden or characterisation test and no output hash, so the physical module move was never proved output-neutral. Worse, one of the three boundary rules is baselined open: hermes-outside-adapter grandfathers 21 crossings across 13 files, including src/app/page.tsx, so that boundary is a counter, not a contract, and the doctrine's own line applies to it verbatim.

rulings.ruling: B (raw SQL behind a repository layer)
rulings.note: PatterStage owns all 49 of its tables, carries no ORM anywhere in its dependency tree, and already routes persistence through 16 hand-written *-repository.ts modules over better-sqlite3.
rulings.conflict: B's whole claim is hand-written SQL in one place, and the seam is breached: src/app/api/agents/route.ts, src/app/api/monitor/route.ts and src/app/api/sessions/[id]/route.ts call prepare() directly, so three route handlers hold SQL the repository layer does not know about.

rulings.ruling: A (always computed), with B for the config read
rulings.note: src/lib/stats/derive.ts takes no DB and no IO by design, and with one operator against local SQLite there is no read rate at which storage beats drift; nothing here carries attestation weight, so C never triggers.
rulings.conflict: None on the ruling; this is the one wargame PatterStage already answers to spec. The narrow gap: config-cache.ts is a correct B (explicit invalidate plus a 15s TTL backstop) but only PatterStage's own PUT /api/config invalidates it, while the agent and any hand edit to ~/.hermes/config.yaml are a second writer with no invalidation path, leaving the TTL as the sole owner.

rulings.ruling: B (durable database claim queue)
rulings.note: orchestration/scheduler/tick.ts already claims each occurrence with a deterministic run id whose PK guard rejects a duplicate tick, and recomputes due work from next_run_at rather than an in-memory timer, which is B's substance on SQLite's guarantees.
rulings.conflict: Deep Research sits on A inside that B system: research-repository.ts states runResearchJob is fire-and-forget with no rebuildable unit, so boot recovery can only mark an interrupted run failed. That fails the rule's own test, because the LLM spend a dead research run consumed is unrecoverable and the operator's standing constraint is no spend without his approval.

rulings.ruling: C (one language, shared source)
rulings.note: TypeScript sits on both sides of every seam, components and route handlers import the same type modules (@/types/chat, @/lib/analytics/event-types), and apiFetch centralises the throw-on-non-2xx discipline that C still owes.
rulings.ownerQuestion: Adopt PatterStudio's tests/fixtures/agentruntime-wire.json as a committed drift gate in this repo, or delete the claim from PatterStudio? Adopting couples a public Apache-2.0 repo's CI to a private repo's fixture (vendoring the file is the cheap version, and it re-opens the seam ADR-0002 deliberately closed); deleting concedes that the two run engines may diverge silently, after ADR-0002 recorded that the convergence already ran out of PatterStage. Either way the mission and template-pack JSON Schemas must be gated regardless, since that costs one CI step and no coupling.
rulings.conflict: C is only legitimate with commit-and-gate discipline for anything leaving the repo, and neither departing artefact is gated. src/lib/schema/json/mission-v1.schema.json and template-pack-v1.schema.json are generated from Zod and committed, yet generate:schema-json runs in no gate, no CI step and no test. Separately, PatterStudio ships tests/fixtures/agentruntime-wire.json asserting that PatterStage's CI consumes the same file, and the only mention of that filename anywhere in this repo is the ADR reporting its absence. Both are direct breaches of architecture doctrine rule 4.

rulings.ruling: B (behaviour pinned first), with C on the seed-pack generator
rulings.note: All 2,279 tests are option A: tests/ holds no snapshot, golden or characterisation test and no output hash, while npm run seed-pack emits deterministic artefacts that no test references at all.
rulings.conflict: This is the sharpest gap in the batch. PatterStage runs on A alone while every restructure it gets is agent-driven, which the rule says A can never prove by itself, and the seed-pack generator is exactly the deterministic-artefact case C exists for yet is wholly untested. CI compounds it: Playwright runs with PLAYWRIGHT_SMOKE=1 so 38 of 42 E2E tests never guard a PR, and the design-lint shrink-only baseline is a debt ratchet, not a behaviour canary. This also blocks WG-ARCH-001, whose C ruling is owed the canary this one would produce.

rulings.ruling: B (owned adapter) for Hermes, C (raw protocol) for the LLM wire
rulings.note: No vendor SDK appears in package.json at all; llm.ts speaks raw fetch through buildDirectRequest/inferApiStyle, and Hermes reaches the app only via the AgentRuntime port with frameworks/registry.ts as the declared swap point.
rulings.conflict: The adapter leaks and the leak is baselined rather than fixed: hermes-outside-adapter grandfathers 21 hits across 13 files, including five API route handlers and four UI components (src/app/page.tsx, GatewayBanner.tsx, ModelEditor.tsx, VersionFooter.tsx), so HERMES_HOME, .hermes/ paths and getActiveHermesPaths sit inside core on a green build. The exit route ADR-0002 writes down is real, but its cost is understated by 13 files the port does not cover.

rulings.ruling: A (one shared database)
rulings.note: One deployable, one operator, one SQLite file backed up before every migration, and ADR-0005 already rules module data ownership logically (prefixed tables, no cross-module reads) so a second physical database would be pure ceremony.
rulings.conflict: Doctrine rule 7 requires every persisted table to name its consumer and its retention plan before it lands, and across 49 tables there is no retention at all: no prune, no TTL and no vacuum anywhere in src/. analytics_events and chat_messages are append-only and unbounded on a machine the operator intends to run this on for years, which is the volume asymmetry the rule wants designed before the feed exists, not after.

rulings.ruling: A. Dark-first, single register (with rec-room's reader as a scoped D exception)
rulings.note: The palette is literally the Cherenkov emission ramp (#33ddff…#0071c2) on a #040b12 ground and there is no `prefers-color-scheme` block, `data-theme` hook or theme toggle anywhere in src/, so the register is already single and luminous.
rulings.conflict: "Single register" is not true today. src/modules/rec-room/components/ReaderSettings.tsx ships four page themes including a full light one (bg #f5f0e8 / text #2c2c2c) and a sepia, hardcoded as raw hexes outside the token system (it sits in the no-raw-colour-in-tsx baseline). That is an undeclared mixed register (option D) shipping inside a module, carrying a second QC surface nobody budgeted for and drifting from @pattertech/ui, which is dark-only.

rulings.ruling: App shell for all 27 routes; long read (article kit) for the two genuine reading surfaces (laboratory/research report, rec-room story reader). No landing, hub or utility archetype exists in this repo.
rulings.note: Every route hangs off one persistent sidebar+main chrome in src/app/layout.tsx and the visitor's verb on all of them is operate, which the decision rule sends straight to app shell.
rulings.conflict: WG-WEB-002 lists app shell as "outside this module's scope today; wargame it when it first appears" — PatterStage IS that first appearance, so the module has no vocabulary for the archetype covering 100% of this venture's surfaces. Concretely, FLOWS.md's linking rules (every page ends in exactly one colophon; detail pages carry a back link to their hub; first-screen contract per archetype) are inapplicable to a sidebar app, and PatterStage obeys none of them. Ruling "app shell" and moving on records the gap; it does not close it. ADR-0001 (hosts WORK not SURFACES) means that gap will never be filled by borrowing the website's archetypes.

rulings.ruling: D (Table) for record surfaces, A (Ledger) for parallel-fact lists, C (Panel) only for the genuinely self-contained thing. Not the card grid.
rulings.note: Sessions, logs, models, missions and skills are records with 3+ comparable fields, which the decision rule sends to a table or a ledger, not to the rounded-xl box the code actually uses at src/app/(main)/sessions/page.tsx:83.
rulings.conflict: This contradicts current practice head-on. The house container is a bordered box — src/components/ui/Card.tsx plus src/components/dashboard/Panel.tsx, 108 `grid-cols-N` sites, and exactly 3 `<table>` elements in the whole of src/ — which is the boxed-card grid Doctrine 5 names as the single strongest generic-template tell. StatPill is precisely what CONTAINERS.md lists under Never for numbers (a bordered, icon-bearing stat card rather than a ruled plaque). The correct exemplar already exists in the repo: src/components/logs/LogRow.tsx renders a hairline-ruled mono grid row, i.e. a ledger, so the pattern is proven here and simply not adopted. None of design-lint's 10 rules can see a card grid, so nothing structural stops the drift (Doctrine 3: the fix is a primitive, not a reminder).

rulings.ruling: B. Concentrated
rulings.note: The one place continuous motion belongs is the live run — `ps-rail-flow` and `ps-edge-glow` on the Composer canvas are the signature animated piece — and src/components/motion/index.tsx already funnels every reveal through a single `useReducedMotion` gate.
rulings.conflict: Continuous motion has leaked outside the signature. `animate-flame` (1.6s infinite) drives a gamification streak badge, `animate-bounce` drives a typing indicator and an import button, and `.animate-shimmer` runs a 2.2s infinite gradient sweep. Doctrine 8 permits loops only as live visuals or on duty cycles of ~12-18s or longer; a 1.6s infinite flame on an achievement badge is neither, and the achievements subsystem is the surface least connected to live agent state. The reduced-motion guard is real (globals.css:169), so the breach is budget scope, not accessibility.

rulings.ruling: C, scoped: fields and conduits in the chrome, radiance kept strictly semantic (live state only); the bloom tier deferred pending the owner call below.
rulings.note: Same brand physics as the v3 worked ruling (identical Cherenkov ramp) but none of the tiers exist here — globals.css has zero radial-gradient fields, zero conduits and no delegated bloom listener, so the console sits at A/B, the exact posture the doctrine's own v2 ruling recorded as reading "Teletext, robotic".
rulings.ownerQuestion: In a console where glow already carries meaning — docs/design-tokens.md reserves pulse-glow/glow-surface for live/active state — how far up does the dimmer go? Option B (fields only): roughly a day of CSS, keeps "glowing = running" unambiguous, and accepts the v2 dead-reads risk on a brand whose story is emitted light. Option C-minus-bloom (fields + conduits in chrome, per the v4 recalibration): the house default one notch down, costs a conduit implementation plus a QC pass on all 27 routes. Full C adds the delegated bloom listener — the tier that competes hardest with "glow = live", needs a fine pointer, and buys the least on a single-operator desktop tool. Which one, given death #2 (a sole dev's budget eaten by work that is not the product)?
rulings.conflict: PatterStage's own written rule ("glow reads as a subtle luminescence on cards, not a flat light source… the reactor-core pulse is reserved for live/active states", globals.css and docs/design-tokens.md) is narrower than Doctrine 2 and, read literally, forbids the ambient field tier the house default requires. One of the two has to give, and today the local rule is winning by default because nobody has noticed the collision. Separately, the doctrine's decision rule offers only "reading-heavy" and "marketing" as scaling categories — it never prices an instrument surface where light is a signal, which is why this one is genuinely forked.

rulings.ruling: Reference-first (tables, ruled lists, anchor-stable headings, minimal theatre), with the dashboard as the single skim-first surface.
rulings.note: Session shape is many short lookups against ~43 tables of operational record rather than one long read, and the dashboard's own header comment states its job is "one-glance situational awareness → one-click actions".
rulings.conflict: Density is currently bought below the legibility floor the project itself set. `no-sub-12px-type` accounts for 370 of the 869 baselined design-lint violations across ~130 files — the largest real category of debt, since the other 449 are em-dashes in docs — and the rule's own text says sub-12px "fails legibility for a dense operator surface and is unreadable at arm's length". docs/UX_AUDIT.md B4 independently flags "reduce the all-caps + mono-everywhere density". Reference-first is the right register, but it has been implemented by shrinking type instead of by ruling rows and fixing the type ladder. Second-order: the operator named BOTH audiences (himself and a stranger installing from scratch), and death #1 turns entirely on the stranger — the expert's density is the newcomer's wall, and no first-run reading aid exists anywhere in the 27 routes.

rulings.ruling: C. Server-rendered app
rulings.note: Auth is enforced in src/proxy.ts, all state is better-sqlite3 at schema v30, and instrumentation.ts opens the DB at boot for the orchestration scheduler — none of which survives a static export.
rulings.conflict: Two things the doctrine gets wrong for this venture. First, option C defers to "a different module of this framework once it exists" — that module does not exist, so the one wargame in web-design that admits PatterStage's shape immediately hands it off to nothing (the same hole as WG-WEB-002). Second, every "it depends on" clause here — traffic shape, free-tier friendliness, immunity to bad requests, "a static export has no runtime to operate" — presumes PatterTech hosts the deployable. PatterStage is installed and run by the user on their own machine and PatterTech hosts nothing, so the hosting axis this wargame turns on is empty. The ruling is right; the reasoning the wargame supplies for it does not apply, and the real constraints (install-script and .exe reliability, SQLite migration safety, Docker non-root) live in devops, not here.

rulings.ruling: B, next/image with the built-in local loader; CDN and third-party transformers barred
rulings.note: PatterStage runs a real Next 16 server (src/proxy.ts, better-sqlite3, instrumentation), not a static export, so request-time optimisation is available, but "no spend without my approval" and "minimal dependencies" bar the CDN half of B.
rulings.conflict: No conflict with today's code: the repo's only binary asset is src/app/favicon.ico, there is no public/ directory, and no or next/image call exists anywhere in src/. That is option C's blessed one-off, correctly. The gap is forward-looking: next.config.ts declares no images.loader and no remotePatterns policy, so nothing in the gate stops the first real image from arriving behind a remote loader. That is death #3 (local-first quietly stops being true) in its exact stated form, one unnoticed decision.

rulings.ruling: B, one registered module-to-accent map of four entries, sourced from the vendored kit
rulings.note: ADR-0005 makes the module the unit and src/lib/modules/registry.ts registers four (core, hermes, laboratory, rec-room), but accent is set per nav link today, so the Hermes module alone flies purple, green, cyan, orange and pink.
rulings.conflict: Yes, three ways. First, there is no map at all: colour is a per-link string literal in registry.ts, so an accent means "this icon" rather than "this venture", which is precisely what B exists to prevent. Second, five accents compete in a single sidebar while docs/design-tokens.md instructs "keep few competing accents per screen" and calls purple/green/pink/orange semantic rather than decorative. Third, B's contrast clause fails outright: I measured --color-neon-purple #8b5cff at 4.44:1 on dark-900 and 4.03:1 on dark-800, both under the 4.5:1 body minimum, and purple is the accent carrying Hermes Operations and Rec Room. ADR-0003 compounds this by ruling those "four extra accents" to be drift, so the map must be rebuilt on @pattertech/ui's Cherenkov ladder, not on today's neon-* set.

rulings.ruling: The house trio: Space Grotesk display, Inter text, JetBrains Mono; restore the missing display face
rulings.note: ADR-0003 (accepted 2026-07-25) orders @pattertech/ui vendored verbatim and its theme.css declares --font-display: "Space Grotesk", while src/app/layout.tsx imports only Inter and JetBrains_Mono.
rulings.conflict: Yes. PatterStage has no display face at all: globals.css @theme declares --font-sans and --font-mono and nothing else, so every h1 renders in the text face and the "trio" is a duo. This is not the inertia the wargame warns against, because PatterStage is not a different brand from PatterStudio, it is the same Cherenkov identity, and ADR-0003 removes the choice. Delivery is safe for local-first: next/font/google self-hosts at build time, so a third family costs no runtime third-party request. One clause of the doctrine must be rejected, though: step 4's "kickers read at 0.7rem tracked" is 11.2px and would violate PatterStage's own no-sub-12px-type law, on a repo already carrying 370 baselined sub-12px violations it is trying to shrink. Take the trio, reject that sizing; a dense operator surface read at arm's length is the reason the local law exists.

rulings.ruling: B, rich hover treatments only; C deferred until the vendored kit ships it
rulings.note: The wargame's own escape clause, "choose B when the team cannot own a shared listener's upkeep", decides it for a sole dev whose named death #2 is the budget going to seams, and ADR-0003 bars minting new design primitives locally.
rulings.conflict: This matches practice (471 hover: utilities in TSX, zero pointer-position listeners, no data-bloom equivalent, reduced motion honoured centrally in src/components/motion/index.tsx), so I want to be explicit that it is not inertia. The brand genuinely IS field physics, which fires C's "brand philosophy includes responsiveness" clause; the only things holding it at B are the upkeep clause and ADR-0003. So this ruling has an expiry: when @pattertech/ui ships a BloomField, PatterStage takes it rather than hand-building one. Also worth recording as a doctrine gap: PatterStage's surface already answers RUN state, not the cursor. pulse-glow, glow-surface and ps-electrified are reserved for live and active states, per the written restraint note in docs/design-tokens.md. That is a presence signal the A-to-D ladder does not name, and for an operator console it is the righter thing to be alive to than the pointer.

rulings.ruling: A, generated only
rulings.note: The whole repo holds one binary (src/app/favicon.ico), every atmosphere is already computed (grid-bg layered gradients, ps-rail-flow, the SVG viz components, glow-*), and an abstract Cherenkov theme is the doctrine's own stated A case.
rulings.conflict: No disagreement with practice, but A is habit here rather than law, and that is a live hole. design-lint carries ten rules and not one of them touches media: no /

rulings.ruling: C, but PatterStage today is A plus C with layer B entirely absent
rulings.note: find src -iname GUIDE.md returns nothing and no component carries a JSDoc law header, so every law string lives in scripts/tooling/design-lint.mjs, one directory away from every file it governs, which is the exact failure mode the wargame describes.
rulings.conflict: Yes, and it is the sharpest finding in this batch. design-lint.mjs's own header cites WG-WEB-013 by name and claims the three-layer ruling, then ships two of the three layers. The proof that B matters is already in the repo: docs/design-tokens.md line 65 still instructs contributors to use --ch-shell-header-min-height, which is the precise pattern lint rule no-ch-custom-properties calls "CSS that silently does nothing". The doc and the lint contradict each other today. Two rules are also under-scoped. no-raw-colour-in-tsx is gated on f.endsWith(".tsx"), so globals.css, the file that DEFINES the palette, is the single file exempt from the colour law; it holds 9 raw rgb()/rgba() literals including the three different cyans REPO_GUIDE already confesses to. And no-sub-12px-type matches only text-[Npx], so text-[0.7rem] (11.2px) passes unseen; zero instances exist today, so that one is latent rather than live. The shrink-only baseline at 869 is good discipline and should stay; the missing layer is colocation, not enforcement.

rulings.ruling: A, media is a citation in the reading column
rulings.note: All three of the wargame's dependencies are genuinely dead here: there is no media (both markdown renderers escapeHtml first and implement no image syntax), no band system (w-screen/100vw/bleed finds only a max-w-screen-xl container cap), and so no content-versus-pacing block to place.
rulings.conflict: Nothing contradicts A, because B is currently unreachable rather than rejected: renderMarkdown in src/lib/chat-utils.ts and renderReportHtml in src/lib/laboratory/deep-research/markdown.ts both escape all HTML and support only fences, inline code, bold, italic, links and lists, so a model returning an image renders as a link, not a picture. The adjacent law that DOES fail is measure rather than placement, and it is worth the owner knowing: the longest-form content PatterStage produces, the deep-research report, renders through a PROSE constant in src/components/research/ResearchReport.tsx that sets no max-width, and the artifacts viewer uses prose max-w-none. The reading column that makes "citation" mean anything is held on only one of the three longform surfaces, the Story Weaver reader at max-w-3xl.

rulings.ruling: B. Floors per surface, ratchet-only-up, set from today's honest measurement, not from the current placeholder numbers.
rulings.note: CI already runs test:coverage on two runners and the honest measurement exists today (src/lib 69.75% statements, src/lib/runtime 87.92%, src/components 34.69%), which is already the doctrine's engine-above-service-above-UI ordering.
rulings.conflict: Yes, twice over. First, the floors are decoration: jest.config.js sets global 10/8/5/10 and src/lib 15/12/8/15 (statements/branches/functions/lines) against a measured 54.7% global and 69.75% src/lib, roughly 4.6x below reality, so no regression a human would notice can trip them. Second, the ratchet has already run backwards: commit 0e3fef9b, titled 'fix: lower coverage thresholds to match current test coverage' with the body 'Lowered thresholds to 4% ... to unblock CI', is a floor moved down to make a red gate pass. That violates delivery rule 2, rule 6, and PatterStage's own CLAUDE.md prohibition on weakening a failing check. Third, collectCoverageFrom excludes src/app/** entirely, so every one of the ~38 API route groups is unmeasured and cannot be assigned a band at all. Worth naming: the venture already runs the correct mechanism elsewhere. design-lint.baseline.json is a per-file, shrink-only allowlist with an explicit 'do NOT run --update-baseline to silence a new violation' guard. Coverage simply does not use the mechanism the same repo already proved it can operate.

rulings.ruling: B. Fast suites gate every change; the full end-to-end acceptance suite, including the install journey, blocks main.
rulings.note: The harness the decision rule requires is already in-repo (mock-hermes, mock-llm and mock-hindsight give synthetic external modes, and playwright.config.ts boots a production next start on an isolated CH_DATA_DIR), so only wiring separates PatterStage from B.
rulings.conflict: Yes. There is no trunk tier at all. ci.yml fires an identical job set on push and pull_request to both main and dev, and the e2e-smoke job pins PLAYWRIGHT_SMOKE=1, whose testMatch is '**/smoke.spec.ts'. Twelve of the thirteen spec files therefore run nowhere in CI, on any branch. docs/TESTING.md is candid that the rest is a human chore: 'Pre-release: Run the full navigation matrix locally ... CI does not run the full matrix on every push.' That is a habit, not a gate. Worse for rule 5: the only real assembled proof, the real-hermes-integration job, is gated 'if: github.event_name == push', so a dev to main merge is proven after it lands rather than before, which inverts 'the trunk takes assembled proof'. And the journey guarding the venture's number-one cheapest death, a stranger installing from scratch, is tests/integration/test_full_install_update_process.py, which TESTING.md states outright is 'not part of CI, run it manually before releases'. Note also that the current Playwright specs are render assertions ('heading is visible'), not journeys; missions-runtime.spec.ts says so in its own header comment. Encoding B means writing the acceptance journeys, not just lifting PLAYWRIGHT_SMOKE.

rulings.ruling: B. Component states, pixel-exact, zero threshold, rendered in a pinned container, baselines committed and re-baselining a reviewed event.
rulings.note: A styled kit exists (24 primitives in src/components/ui plus a field kit), and option A's predicted drift has already been paid: ADR-0003 records the hand-ported tokens producing shipped defects, two dead Tailwind classes and a hover treatment Tailwind never compiles.
rulings.ownerQuestion: Are the first pixel baselines cut against today's hand-rolled src/components/ui, or only after ADR-0003 Part 1 vendors @pattertech/ui into src/kit/ (which does not exist on disk yet)? Baselining now buys the gate immediately and costs one full re-baseline the day the vendored kit lands. Waiting costs nothing up front but makes the VRT gate hostage to an ADR that is accepted and unexecuted, which is exactly the mechanism by which option A persists indefinitely. If you choose to wait, the honest form is a dated deadline in the lock-book, not the phrase 'when src/kit lands'.
rulings.conflict: Yes. PatterStage has no visual gate of any kind. grep across the tree finds zero toHaveScreenshot, toMatchSnapshot, Storybook, Lost Pixel, Percy or Chromatic, and there is no styleguide surface enumerating component states, so B needs a surface built before it needs a tool chosen. The only screenshot machinery, tests/e2e/screenshots.spec.ts, is opt-in doc-image capture that takes fullPage shots after a bare waitForTimeout(1500) with no comparison at all, which is the precise non-deterministic shape this wargame names as how the gate goes soft. What substitutes for the gate today is a person: docs/QA_NOTES.md exists only because 'two consecutive walkthroughs flagged a cluster of broken widgets that are code-correct in the current source'. The venture is already paying manual visual-QA cost and receiving false positives in return, which is the strongest available argument that the pixel gate is owed.

rulings.ruling: C. Determinism first, zero retries on blocking gates, with B (quarantine plus a filed order and a deadline) as the only containment valve.
rulings.note: The live flake is exactly the class rule 4 names: six next/font/google families across two layouts make next build fetch a CDN inside CI, and ci.yml's own comment admits Turbopack 'treats the failure as a hard error'.
rulings.conflict: Yes, and this is the sharpest conflict in the batch. playwright.config.ts sets 'retries: process.env.CI ? 1 : 0', an automatic retry on the only blocking browser gate, which this wargame forbids in terms ('A is forbidden on blocking gates'), and 'trace: on-first-retry' shows the retry is the designed debugging path rather than an accident. Around it ci.yml stacks four more retry mechanisms: a checkout with continue-on-error plus a duplicate retry step, 'npm ci || (npm cache clean --force && npm ci)', a three-attempt curl warmup of six Google Fonts URLs, and 'npm run build || (sleep 5; npm run build)' whose comment states plainly that it exists to survive a known flake. The estate has already bought this fix once: WiseWattage's ruling was no CDN downloads in CI. The part that makes this more than CI hygiene: scripts/bootstrap/setup.sh line 211 runs npm run build, there is no public/fonts and no local font fallback, so a stranger installing PatterStage on a machine without egress to fonts.googleapis.com gets a hard build failure. The determinism debt and cheapest death number three (local-first quietly stops being true) are the same defect, and it is currently disguised as a flaky macOS job.

rulings.ruling: B - snapshots plus a scheduled restore test, with recorded evidence
rulings.note: Production data exists at schema v30 across ~43 tables and backups are written in three places, yet grep for pre-migrate/pre-baseline/.bak across src, scripts and tests returns only writers: no restore script, no restore path, and zero restore tests among 2,279.
rulings.conflict: Direct contradiction. PatterStage is at option A today, which the wargame says is "acceptable only before production data exists" and which it counts as a gap rather than evidence. It is worse than the WiseWattage case it cites, because PatterStage does not merely trust a provider's snapshots, it ships its own destructor: src/lib/db/upgrade.ts:300 backs the DB up to patterstage.db.pre-baseline-<ts>, recreates it from 001_baseline.sql, and re-imports 11 named tables (credentials, models, model_defaults, model_fallbacks, fallback_config, missions, cron_jobs, sessions, stories, sync_registry, gateway_platforms) out of ~43. Runs, schedules, chat, artifacts, deep-research, rec-room and analytics survive only inside a file no code path can read back, and docs/MIGRATION.md:83 substitutes a human instruction ("review the backup before deleting it") for the missing capability. This runs on machines belonging to people the operator has never met, so the loss is not his to accept.

rulings.ruling: B (budget with approval gates) with C (hard caps) layered on unattended agent work
rulings.note: The wargame's unattended-fleet trigger fires on mission-queue-tick.ts, composer-tick.ts, host-scheduler.ts and deep-research/run-job.ts, which dispatch inference with no ceiling, while the only money in the system is retrospective: model-cost.ts estimateCost summed into the Laboratory Insights dollar total.
rulings.conflict: PatterStage today is A with a dashboard. It has the reporting half of B (a hardcoded rate card in src/lib/analytics/model-cost.ts, spend aggregated in run-aggregates.ts, a total displayed on the Insights page) and none of the governing half: no monthly figure anywhere, no approval gate, no cap, no triage pause. Every `budget` identifier in src is a time or round budget (retry, staleness, deep-research rounds, Hindsight reflect), never a spend budget, and the sole cost_usd column sits in 014_benchmarks.sql, the subsystem ADR-0004 records as deleted. That contradicts the operator's own stated rule, "No spend without my approval," which is currently enforced by nothing but his attention. Two facts the wargame's framing does not carry: local OpenAI-compatible providers are a first-class path (llm-endpoint.ts), so a zero-spend configuration genuinely exists and spend is opt-in, which lowers urgency for his own install; but PatterStage ships, so the money an unattended loop burns is a stranger's, and the wargame's "whose money is it" axis has no row for a user you have never met. Also note its instruction that tier cliffs are design inputs belonging in WG-ARCH-008: PatterStage's equivalent knobs (context size, round count, retry budget) are all tuned for latency, never for cost.

rulings.ruling: C - self-hosting, ruled because sovereignty is the product; the host is the user's machine, not the venture's
rulings.note: The decision rule reserves C for when sovereignty is the product, and local-first is the opening clause of the operator-confirmed restatement plus cheapest death #3, verified live rather than aspirational because llm-endpoint.ts supports local OpenAI-compatible endpoints (LM Studio, Ollama, vLLM) so a zero-remote configuration runs today.
rulings.conflict: No conflict with practice, but the wargame's option set does not fit and saying so is the point. All three options assume the venture pays for and operates the runtime; PatterStage's runtime cost and pager transfer wholesale to the user, so there is no account, no region, no root holder and no trust audience to rule on. The doctrine's own warning against C, "a standing ops tax no solo-operator venture pays willingly," is not escaped here so much as exported, and that export is the exact mechanism of cheapest death #1. One dependency the ruling should not leave implicit: the venture is not hosting-free, it is concentrated on GitHub, which holds the repo, the CI, the distribution channel and the update path, since ps-deploy update does git fetch plus git reset --hard origin/<branch> against github.com. Local-first holds at runtime; it does not hold for updates. Separately, the unresolved LICENSE-versus-GitHub-metadata contradiction (Apache-2.0 in the repo, MIT in GitHub's metadata) sits on that same single point of dependency.

rulings.ruling: C - mixed, but inverted: the stateful app ships as a native host install, the container is the CI parity rig
rulings.note: docs/DEPLOY.md:81 and :83 make the native build the primary artefact and Docker "optional... required in CI only", and the app cannot be container-only because its job is to drive the host (~/.hermes, host git, crontab and schtasks, lsof port kill, ps-deploy restarting the host process).
rulings.ownerQuestion: Does a stranger installing PatterStage get a third deployment model, and if so which? Today there are two (git clone plus install.sh building natively, and an optional Docker image exercised only by the CI docker-image job). The interview names a "dedicated install .exe" as the fix for cheapest death #1, but install.ps1 is a 22-line stub that refuses native Windows and redirects to WSL2 per the Linux-first ruling, so the .exe as described cannot be built without reversing that. Three options, with costs. (1) Keep two models and make install.sh the only supported stranger path: costs nothing new, leaves death #1 unmitigated, and clone-and-run stays the bar. (2) Promote the container to the shipped artefact: buys parity by construction on a machine you have never seen, but the Dockerfile already pays a visible tax to emulate a host (it installs bash, git, curl, iproute2, psmisc and socat into the runtime layer) and still cannot run update or rebuild because .dockerignore excludes .git, so host-driving features degrade. (3) Build the .exe: directly addresses death #1, and costs a third failure vocabulary for a sole dev plus a reversal of the Linux-first platform decision, since a Windows installer that shells out to WSL2 is a fourth thing to support, not a simpler third.
rulings.conflict: The doctrine's C is inverted here and its decision rule's premise fails. C as written means the API is containerised and static fronts ride their platform; PatterStage has one surface with one deploy and no static front, and its mix is the reverse, with the stateful app native and the container serving as a test harness. The rule that "the API is always a container (it is the part that must move one day)" is violated by design: this app never moves, it is installed. The parity trigger the wargame uses to force A does fire, and hard, because every install is a handover to unseen hardware, but the artefact that needs parity proof is the native install and CI proves the wrong one: the docker-image job builds and smokes the image on every PR while boot-smoke covers only cross-platform primitives with no app build, so nothing in CI exercises install.sh end to end on a clean machine. Compounding it, the E2E suite that would catch a broken install runs smoke-only (PLAYWRIGHT_SMOKE=1), leaving 38 of 42 tests off every PR.

findings.problem: The premise the inheritance rests on is false. The ruling's note reads "All three of the wargame's dependencies are genuinely dead here: there is no media", and "B is currently unreachable rather than rejected". That is true of the app's runtime renderers and false of the venture. PatterStage ships seven git-tracked PNG screenshots in docs/images/ (688 KB; 8 tracked binaries totalling 713,737 bytes), embedded as markdown images at README.md:9 and at six points in docs/USER_WALKTHROUGH_GUIDE.md (lines 69, 156, 276, 323, 381, 736). Those two files are the venture's longest-form shipped documents (197 and 1,228 lines) and, under this same walk's WG-VOX-001 ruling, both are B product surfaces. The same fact falsifies two premises the walk marked argued: WG-WEB-008's "the repo's only binary asset is src/app/favicon.ico" and WG-WEB-012's "the whole repo holds one binary (src/app/favicon.ico)". findings.evidence: `git ls-files` binary listing: docs/images/{agent-profiles,chat,dashboard,insights,missions-board,models-config,skills-manager}.png plus src/app/favicon.ico; `du -sh docs/images/` = 688K; total tracked binary bytes 713,737 across 8 files. Markdown references: README.md:9 `![PatterStage dashboard](docs/images/dashboard.png)` and docs/USER_WALKTHROUGH_GUIDE.md:69,156,276,323,381,736. `ls -d public` returns no such directory (so WG-WEB-008's public/ claim holds; its "only binary asset" claim does not). No route reads docs/*.md, so this is a repo-and-GitHub surface rather than an in-app one, which is exactly why the src/-scoped search missed it.

The ruling will very likely still be A (GitHub's renderer offers no band, so citation is structurally forced), but that is a conclusion to reach rather than assume, and it turns three sentences of dead reasoning into a live one. Separately correct the "one binary" premise in the WG-WEB-008 and WG-WEB-012 notes, and record the 688 KB as the clone-weight fact it is, under death #1, rather than as the hypothetical WG-WEB-012 currently describes.

findings.problem: `auth` is a recorded PatterStage trigger that names no wargame anywhere in the corpus, so it did no work in the walk. docs/VENTURE_BRIEF.md lists it as present ("**auth** (single-operator bearer token in `src/proxy.ts`)") and the phase B scale ruling leans on it explicitly ("Server state + auth + standing ops force >= M"), yet across all 33 wargames no front-matter carries an `auth` tag. The only `security` tag in the estate is WG-ARCH-007 (`arch, infra, security`), which rules on vendor SDK versus owned adapter and never touches access control. The result: 31 phase-C rulings, and not one of them rules on the venture's authentication posture, despite src/proxy.ts being the single enforcement point for the whole app, despite CLAUDE.md carrying a standing prohibition built around it ("Never add an authentication check to a route handler"), and despite the most recent security commit on this branch being `fix(security): real authentication, and close the unauthenticated RCE chain (Phase S1)` — i.e. this is the subsystem that most recently failed. This is the same silent failure the lens hunts, arriving by the opposite route: not a wargame inherited when a trigger named it, but a trigger that names nothing, so nobody thought about it and the omission leaves no trace in the lock-book. WALK_ORDER has the remedy at lines 62-67 (file a draft wargame in docs/EOS_FEEDBACK.md, record the ruling as WG-DRAFT-NNN, the harvest assigns a real id later). It was not used: docs/EOS_FEEDBACK.md does not exist in PatterStage and no WG-DRAFT row appears in the walk.
findings.evidence: docs/VENTURE_BRIEF.md "Scale and triggers" section. `grep -n '^tags:' doctrine/*/wargames/*.md` filtered for auth|security returns exactly one line: doctrine/architecture/wargames/WG-ARCH-007-vendor-seams.md:4 `tags: [arch, infra, security]`. WARGAME_INDEX confirms the full tag vocabulary across all 33 rows contains no `auth`. inception/WALK_ORDER.md:62-67. `ls docs/EOS_FEEDBACK.md` in PatterStage: no such file. Recent commit f1aadc2 lineage includes `fix(security): real authentication, and close the unauthenticated RCE chain (Phase S1)`.
findings.fix: File the draft wargame WALK_ORDER already prescribes — the access-control question (single shared secret / per-actor credentials / delegated identity, and where enforcement lives) with PatterStage's proxy.ts ruling as its first worked entry — into docs/EOS_FEEDBACK.md, and record it in the lock-book as WG-DRAFT-001. This is the one case in the walk where the correct output is a new wargame rather than a ruling, and it costs one file. Without it the estate's next M venture with auth inherits the same blind spot with no record that anyone noticed.

findings.problem: PatterStage's trigger set was never recorded in the vocabulary the walk-build rule operates on, so no argued/inherited label in this walk can be checked by a later reader — which is the mechanism by which F1 went unnoticed. WALK_ORDER steps 2 and 3 require collecting "the domains and trigger tags the interview surfaced" and then keeping a wargame if "any of its tags is in the trigger set", a tag-to-tag operation. What docs/VENTURE_BRIEF.md actually records is six prose facts: "server state", "auth", "standing ops", "web surface", "written surfaces", and a "years" lifespan. Only "web surface" maps cleanly onto the index's tag vocabulary {arch, tooling, data, state, infra, ci, testing, security, delivery, web, ops, hosting, money, voice, content, brand, colour, nav, layout, density, motion, media, perf, typography, imagery}. Nothing in the repository states that `media`, `layout`, `content`, `density`, `nav`, `colour`, `typography`, `motion`, `perf`, `brand`, `ci`, `testing`, `tooling` or `security` are triggers, even though all fourteen web wargames and every delivery wargame were walked on that basis. The consequence is asymmetric and bad: the labels cannot be audited, so an over-strict label costs nothing visible and an under-strict one (F1) is invisible until someone re-derives the trigger set by hand, as this review had to.
findings.evidence: inception/WALK_ORDER.md:16-23 (build the walk, tag matching) and INCEPTION.md Phase A ("The output is the venture brief content and the trigger list") plus INTERVIEW.md ("the output fills docs/VENTURE_BRIEF.md and the trigger list for the walk", "Read the trigger list back as plain yes-or-no facts"). docs/VENTURE_BRIEF.md "Scale and triggers" holds the six prose triggers and no tag list. `grep -rn 'trigger set' *.md doctrine inception` across the EOS repo returns only WALK_ORDER's own three references; no venture file anywhere records a tag-form trigger set.
findings.fix: Add the tag-form trigger set to docs/VENTURE_BRIEF.md as one line next to the prose triggers, drawn from the same vocabulary WARGAME_INDEX uses, and note which triggers the scale ruling attached versus which the interview surfaced. It costs a line and makes every argued/inherited label in the lock-book falsifiable. Worth feeding back to the EOS: WALK_ORDER requires the artefact and no template asks for it in the form the rule needs.

findings.problem: The walk ran 31 phase-C rulings (33 including the two phase-B EOS rulings) against WALK_ORDER's own stop condition of twenty, and WG-EOS-001 was not re-run. The rule is unconditional: "A walk running past twenty rulings means the trigger set is wrong (too broad) or the venture is bigger than its scale ruling; stop and re-run WG-EOS-001 before continuing." The walk continued for eleven rulings past the line and recorded neither diagnosis. This belongs to this lens because trigger-set breadth is the input that decides which rulings must be argued: a set broad enough to pull in every wargame in the estate is also a set nobody can spot-check, and the one ruling that escaped argument is the fourteenth and last of the web module. I want to be fair to the doctrine here rather than overstate the walk's fault: WALK_ORDER's budget section is internally inconsistent, since "even S runs twelve to eighteen rulings" and "M and L add the modules their triggers pull in" cannot both hold under a twenty-ruling ceiling — an M venture that walks web plus architecture plus delivery plus devops arithmetically cannot come in under twenty. So the honest reading is that exactly one of three things is true: the trigger set is too broad, the M scale ruling is wrong, or the budget rule is miscalibrated for M and should be fed back. The finding is that the walk recorded none of the three and simply carried on.
findings.evidence: inception/WALK_ORDER.md:68-75 (Budget). Ruling count from the phase C output: 1 voice (WG-VOX-001) + 8 architecture (WG-ARCH-001..008) + 14 web-design (WG-WEB-001..014, split across the walk's `web-design` and `web-b` batches) + 4 delivery (WG-DEL-001..004) + 4 devops (WG-OPS-001..004) = 31; WARGAME_INDEX holds 33 rows total, so the walk took every wargame in the estate. docs/VENTURE_BRIEF.md records the scale as M with no re-rule after the walk.
findings.fix: Record the diagnosis rather than the ruling count. Most likely honest answer given the evidence: the budget rule is miscalibrated for M and should be fed back to the EOS (an M venture with a web surface walks the whole corpus by construction), with the trigger-set breadth confirmed deliberate in the same line. If instead the operator judges the set too broad, that is a re-run of WG-EOS-001 before phase D, not after. Either way the lock-book should carry one sentence saying the ceiling was crossed knowingly, because a stop condition that is passed in silence is a stop condition the next walk will pass in silence too.

audits.lens: Rulings that flatter the status quo — where the walk graded PatterStage's existing arrangement as conformant while the doctrine's own decision rule demanded something else

findings.problem: WG-ARCH-001 ruled C ("the tree is the architecture") when the doctrine makes C conditional on a canary that does not exist, and when option B — the fallback the doctrine actually prescribes — is not achieved either. C is the one option that requires PatterStage to do nothing: src/modules/ already exists.
findings.evidence: WG-ARCH-001-boundary-enforcement.md decision rule: "Move to C when a canary exists that proves moves are output-neutral, and do the move in one reviewed change"; default: "B, rising to C once a canary exists." Its "It depends on" names the precondition explicitly: "Whether a proof of harmless movement exists (tests or an output canary)." Then make B true: hermes-outside-adapter carries no baseline on the boundary it is the sole enforcement for. findings.problem: WG-WEB-001's argued line rests on a premise its own conflict paragraph disproves, and the ruling then converts the disproving evidence into a blessed exception. Ruling the rec-room reader "a scoped D exception" makes shipped, untokenised, undeclared drift conformant by naming it, and mislabels which option it is.
findings.evidence: The argued line claims "there is no `prefers-color-scheme` block, `data-theme` hook or theme toggle anywhere in src/, so the register is already single." grep confirms no prefers-color-scheme and no data-theme, but a theme toggle does exist: src/modules/rec-room/components/ReaderSettings.tsx:11 declares `pageTheme: "dark" | "black" | "sepia" | "light"`, :29-34 hardcodes four palettes as raw hex (light = bg #f5f0e8 / text #2c2c2c), :140 renders the user-facing picker, and :47-58 persists the choice to localStorage. Per WG-WEB-001-surface-register.md's own definitions that is option C, "Dual register (theme switch): User choice, twice the surface to design, test and QC" — not D, which is a fixed design decision ("dark chrome, light reading surfaces"). The decision rule for C is unambiguous: "Choose C only with a demonstrated dual-context audience." The venture has one operator on one desktop console. Separately, ADR-0003 rules that "PatterStage stops minting design tokens immediately" and the four palettes sit in the no-raw-colour-in-tsx baseline.
findings.fix: Correct the option letter (this is C, not D) and rule it out rather than in: the reader's four hardcoded themes are undeclared drift under a ruling of A, and ADR-0003 forbids minting the tokens they are made of. Either delete the light and sepia themes and hold the reader on the Cherenkov ladder, or record a dated deviation with the second QC surface budgeted and the palettes moved into the vendored kit. Do not leave "scoped exception" in the ruling line — that is the phrasing by which drift becomes law.

findings.problem: WG-WEB-011 ruled B while conceding the clause that forces C fires, then deferred C to a component that does not exist in the repo it defers to and is not planned there. Both supporting arguments fail on inspection: the doctrine's escape clause is about team capacity, and ADR-0003 restricts tokens, not components. B is what src/ already does — 471 hover utilities, zero pointer listeners.
findings.evidence: WG-WEB-011-surface-reactivity-budget.md decision rule: "If the brand's philosophy includes responsiveness or field physics, choose C with B's treatments as its base layer. That clause is brand physics, not house habit." The walk agrees the clause fires ("The brand genuinely IS field physics, which fires C's clause"), then rules B. The doctrine sizes C as trivial — default: "C for house projects; it is one small file and one attribute per component" — and a working implementation already exists in the estate: PatterTech_Website/src/components/ui/BloomField.tsx is 66 lines, one rAF-throttled delegated listener, with fine-pointer and reduced-motion opt-outs built in. The deferral target is empty: `grep -rl "BloomField|data-bloom"` across PatterStudio (including shared/ui, the @pattertech/ui kit at shared/ui/src: Logomark.tsx, feedback.tsx, inputs.tsx, overlay.tsx, primitives.tsx/css, theme.css, toast.tsx, utils.ts) returns nothing, so "when @pattertech/ui ships a BloomField" is an unbounded wait on unscheduled work. And ADR-0003's operative sentence is "PatterStage stops minting design tokens immediately. Any new token is a change to the shared kit" — tokens, not a client-side listener; the walk broadened it to "design primitives" to reach B. Practice today confirms B is the zero-work option: 471 `hover:` utilities in TSX, 0 pointermove/onPointerMove/mousemove handlers anywhere in src/.
findings.fix: Either rule C and vendor BloomField.tsx from PatterTech_Website alongside the ADR-0003 kit copy-in (66 lines, same estate, same Cherenkov system, no new upkeep to own), or hold B and make the expiry real: a dated condition in the lock-book plus an order against @pattertech/ui to add the bloom tier, not the phrase "when the vendored kit ships it." Also drop the ADR-0003 justification — it does not cover components. Note this compounds with WG-WEB-005, where the bloom tier was also deferred; two rulings in the same walk defer the same tier, which is how an option becomes permanent by default.

findings.problem: WG-OPS-002 states in its own conflict text that the trigger forcing option A fires "and hard," then rules C with the doctrine's option letter redefined to describe exactly what PatterStage does today (native install primary, container as a CI rig). Inverting an option's meaning to fit current practice is the ruling equivalent of moving a coverage floor down.
findings.evidence: WG-OPS-002-containers.md decision rule: "Handover or parity clauses in force, or a cloud estate ruled by WG-OPS-001: A, one model, local harness running the same images." The walk's own text: "The parity trigger the wargame uses to force A does fire, and hard, because every install is a handover to unseen hardware." It then rules "C - mixed, but inverted," acknowledging "The doctrine's C is inverted here and its decision rule's premise fails." The consequence is visible in CI: .github/workflows/ci.yml has a `docker-image` job that builds and smoke-tests the image on every PR (line 224), while `boot-smoke` (line 157) covers only cross-platform primitives with no app build, and `real-hermes-integration` is gated `if: github.event_name == 'push'` (line 252) so it runs after a merge, not before. Nothing in CI runs scripts/bootstrap/install.sh end to end. The artefact CI proves is the one the ruling calls a test harness; the artefact strangers receive is proven by nobody.
findings.fix: Do not rule an inverted option letter. Either rule A and make the install the one model CI proves (an install.sh job on a clean container image, gating PRs), or record this as a named deviation from WG-OPS-002 with the reason (the app drives the host: ~/.hermes, host git, crontab/schtasks, port kill, ps-deploy restart) and the compensating control written down — which must be a CI job that exercises the native install, since that is the artefact carrying cheapest death #1.

findings.problem: WG-WEB-006 names the dashboard as "the single skim-first surface." The dashboard already does this job by its own header comment, so the ruling costs nothing — and the word "single" forecloses an unconditional doctrine requirement that would have cost work on the surface that needs it.
findings.evidence: WG-WEB-006-density-and-audience.md decision rule opens: "Every long read gets the skim layer anyway (the takeaways band); the fork is how much pacing machinery follows." It is not conditional on the register chosen. The same walk's WG-WEB-002 ruling designates the laboratory/research report and the rec-room story reader as "the two genuine reading surfaces (long read, article kit)." Neither has a skim layer: src/components/research/ResearchReport.tsx renders the whole report through one PROSE constant at :43 applied at :97 (`dangerouslySetInnerHTML`), and grep for "In brief"/takeaway across src/components/research/ and src/app/laboratory returns nothing. The deep-research report is also the venture's longest generated artefact and, per WG-OPS-004, the most expensive one to produce.
findings.fix: Amend the ruling to "reference-first, with the dashboard skim-first and the mandatory takeaways band on both long-read surfaces." A generated report that cost real LLM spend and cannot be skimmed is the one place the skim layer pays for itself — and it is the surface a stranger meets when judging whether the product works.

findings.problem: WG-ARCH-004 credited PatterStage with already having "B's substance" and scoped the A-shaped defect to Deep Research alone. B's third named component — a unit-builder registry that rebuilds work from persisted context — is absent from the whole system, not just from research runs; boot recovery re-fails, it never rebuilds.
findings.evidence: WG-ARCH-004-job-execution.md option B: "A jobs table claimed with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, idempotency keys, stale-claim reaping, and a unit-builder registry (closures do not serialise; persist context, rebuild work from it)." PatterStage has the idempotent claim (src/lib/orchestration/scheduler/tick.ts:28, deterministic occurrence id with a PK guard) and a reconcile tick, but no rebuildable unit anywhere. src/lib/orchestration/run-reconcile.ts:236-253 is the whole of boot recovery: runs without a backend id are marked `"failed"` with `"PatterStage restarted before the run was submitted"` and the mission is finalised failed. Durability for the rest is borrowed, not owned — the header at :237-239 says runs survive "because HTTP runs survive a CH restart," i.e. because the Hermes backend holds them, not because the queue can reconstitute them. src/lib/laboratory/deep-research/research-repository.ts:141 records the same posture for research ("runResearchJob is fire-and-forget"), and src/instrumentation.ts:63-71 does the matching re-fail there.
findings.fix: Keep B, but restate what B is owed: a unit-builder registry that persists each dispatched unit's context and rebuilds it on boot, applied to mission runs, composer node runs and research jobs alike — not a Deep Research patch. Until that exists the honest ruling is the doctrine's default, "A with B's seam designed in," plus the note that current durability is the agent backend's property and disappears with it.

findings.problem: WG-ARCH-005 raises a FORK on a question an accepted, owner-signed ADR already answers, and its framing misreads that ADR. The fork asks "Adopt PatterStudio's tests/fixtures/agentruntime-wire.json as a committed drift gate in this repo, or delete the claim from PatterStudio?" and argues adopting "re-opens the seam ADR-0002 deliberately closed". ADR-0002 does not close that seam; it orders the adoption.
findings.evidence: C:/Users/Daniel/Documents/Coding/Github/PatterStage/docs/adr/0002-run-engine-ownership.md, Decision item 3 (status: accepted by Daniel, 2026-07-25): "PatterStage adopts `agentruntime-wire.json` as a merge gate, closing the convergence gate from its own side without waiting for the other." What ADR-0002 closed is the runtime dependency (Alternatives rejected: "Consume PatterStack's engine as written... it would make the public product depend on a private repo"), not the fixture gate. The walk's own conflict text says "the only mention of that filename anywhere in this repo is the ADR reporting its absence" — I grepped the whole tree and the ADR is indeed the only hit (lines 34 and 51), but line 51 is an order, not a report. CLAUDE.md is explicit: "A decision recorded there wins over anything you infer from the code."
findings.fix: Withdraw the adopt-or-delete axis of the fork. Re-file it as a conflict: ADR-0002 decision 3 is accepted and unexecuted, zero implementation in .github/, tests/ or scripts/. If the coupling cost (public Apache-2.0 CI consuming a private repo's fixture) is now judged unacceptable, that is an amendment to ADR-0002, which the ADR process handles — not a fresh wargame fork. The mission-v1/template-pack-v1 JSON Schema gate the fork also names is unaffected and stands on its own.

findings.problem: WG-ARCH-001 is marked argued (needsOwner=false) but ruled C against its own decision rule's stated precondition, and the wargame that supplies that precondition was ruled behind it. The canonical order is inverted, and the walk's own text admits the consequence without changing the ruling.
findings.evidence: WG-ARCH-001-boundary-enforcement.md decision rule: "Move to C when a canary exists that proves moves are output-neutral, and do the move in one reviewed change"; and "Agents in the workforce or a second consumer of any shared layer: at least B, from the first week." The canary is WG-ARCH-006's entire subject. WG-ARCH-006, ruled afterwards, establishes there is none: I grepped tests/ and src/ for toMatchSnapshot, toMatchInlineSnapshot, toHaveScreenshot and __snapshots__ and found zero hits and zero snapshot directories. So the C branch's condition is false and the B branch's condition (agent-driven) is true. The walk states the collision itself under WG-ARCH-006 ("This also blocks WG-ARCH-001, whose C ruling is owed the canary this one would produce") yet leaves WG-ARCH-001 at C, argued. It is worse than one hop: the UI half of that canary is WG-DEL-003, which is FORKED and unresolved, so an argued ruling rests on an open owner question two hops downstream.
findings.fix: Re-rule WG-ARCH-001 as B (machine contract over the current layout) with C recorded as the target, conditional on the canary landing — which is what the decision rule actually produces today. Or mark it needsOwner and bind it explicitly to the WG-DEL-003 fork. Either way, move WG-ARCH-006 ahead of WG-ARCH-001 in the canonical order, because the former's ruling is the latter's input.

findings.problem: Two argued rulings contradict each other on the same fact, and the earlier one (WG-WEB-010) rests its local-first safety claim on a reading the later one (WG-DEL-004) proves false. WG-WEB-010 orders a third Google font family into the root layout on the grounds it is free; WG-DEL-004 finds that the existing Google font families are the venture's determinism defect and its install-time failure mode.
findings.evidence: WG-WEB-010 ruling: "Delivery is safe for local-first: next/font/google self-hosts at build time, so a third family costs no runtime third-party request." That is true of runtime and false of build and install time, which is where this venture pays. Verified: src/app/layout.tsx:2 imports Inter and JetBrains_Mono, src/app/recroom/story-weaver/layout.tsx:1 imports Literata, EB_Garamond, Lora, Merriweather — six families. .github/workflows/ci.yml:111-128 carries a three-attempt curl warmup of exactly those six fonts.googleapis.com URLs, with the comment "Turbopack fetches Google Fonts at build time and treats the failure as a hard error", followed at :145-152 by `npm run build ||` retry whose comment names "the macOS runner's egress to fonts.googleapis.com". scripts/bootstrap/setup.sh:211 runs `npm run build` on the stranger's machine; there is no public/ directory (ls fails) and no committed .woff2 anywhere outside .next/. Space Grotesk would be the seventh CDN fetch on that path. WG-DEL-004's own words: "The determinism debt and cheapest death number three are the same defect."
findings.fix: WG-WEB-010's ruling only survives if it is paired with its delivery cost: vendor the three trio faces as local .woff2 under next/font/local and drop next/font/google. That is WG-DEL-004's prescribed fix anyway ("no CDN downloads in CI", already bought once on WiseWattage), so pairing them costs one change rather than two. If the trio ships on next/font/google, WG-WEB-010's stated justification must be struck and re-argued against the install-time failure, not the runtime one.

findings.problem: WG-WEB-009 is marked argued but B is not what the evidence produces. Its decision rule sends this case to A, ADR-0001 is what makes it an A case, the source the ruling names contains no accent family to map, and B's own gating clause already fails on the measurement the walk itself took.
findings.evidence: WG-WEB-009-brand-family-accents.md decision rule: "Sub-brands with independent identity and published work -> B... Purely topical sections -> A", and "No family at all (one trade, one brand) -> A with a single accent; the map is overhead without imprints." The four entries in src/lib/modules/registry.ts (core, hermes, laboratory, rec-room) are PatterStage's own sections, not sub-brands: ADR-0001 rules that "Every product surface PatterStage references is an external link" and that a product "appears as a row with liveness and an outbound link, never as a nested tree of its pages". ADR-0005's module seam is an internal import boundary, not a brand family. Second, the named source has no accents: PatterStudio/shared/ui/src/theme.css declares one single-hue Cherenkov ramp (--color-cherenkov #33ddff, --color-deep-sky #00bfff, --color-azure #00a1e6, --color-cerulean #008bd1, --color-deep-water #0071c2), one --color-amber, and three semantic tokens (--color-ok, --color-warn, --color-danger). There are no four decorative accents in the kit to build a four-entry map from. Third, the walk measured --color-neon-purple #8b5cff (confirmed at src/app/globals.css:16) at 4.44:1 and 4.03:1, failing B's clause "every accent passing contrast checks on the site's grounds", for the accent proposed to carry two of the four modules.
findings.fix: Re-rule as A: one Cherenkov accent for the whole console, semantic colours (ok/warn/danger) reserved for state, module identity carried by structure and label rather than hue. That is what the decision rule, ADR-0001 and the vendored kit's actual contents jointly produce, and it dissolves the five-competing-accents problem instead of formalising it. If the owner wants module colour anyway, it is a fork — it requires minting accents the kit does not contain, which ADR-0003 forbids doing locally.

findings.problem: WG-WEB-005 sits ahead of WG-WEB-011 despite naming it as an input, and the two rulings then apply ADR-0003 in opposite directions. The consequence lands on the owner: the WG-WEB-005 fork offers a third option that WG-WEB-011, ruled later in the same walk, has already foreclosed.
findings.evidence: WG-WEB-005-ornament-budget.md, It depends on: "The performance floor and touch share (fields and conduits are CSS-cheap; bloom needs fine pointers; see WG-WEB-011)." Its option C is "fields + conduits + bloom + refined neon" — the bloom tier is WG-WEB-011's option C verbatim ("One delegated pointer listener sets local coordinates on the [data-bloom] element"). WG-WEB-005 was ruled in the web-design batch, WG-WEB-011 in the web-b batch after it. WG-WEB-011 then ruled B and deferred C "until the vendored kit ships it", citing "ADR-0003 bars minting new design primitives locally". But WG-WEB-005's fork prices "Option C-minus-bloom... costs a conduit implementation plus a QC pass on all 27 routes" and "Option B (fields only): roughly a day of CSS" — i.e. it prices building field and conduit primitives locally, which is the same bar WG-WEB-011 applied to refuse bloom. ADR-0003 is unambiguous: "PatterStage stops minting design tokens immediately. Any new token is a change to the shared kit, not to globals.css."
findings.fix: Re-order WG-WEB-011 ahead of WG-WEB-005 and re-pose the fork with two live options, not three: full C is already dead by WG-WEB-011's ruling. Then apply ADR-0003 consistently to whichever survives — if fields and conduits are new primitives, the fork's real question is not "how far up the dimmer goes" but "does @pattertech/ui ship these, and if not, who mints them", which is an estate decision on the kit, not a day of CSS in PatterStage.

findings.problem: WG-ARCH-003 (A, always computed) and WG-ARCH-008 (retention plan required for every persisted table) contradict each other, and neither ruling names the other. Executing WG-ARCH-008's remedy silently breaks what ADR-0004 says the progression system exists to show. Both are marked argued.
findings.evidence: WG-ARCH-003 ruled A and rejected C on the grounds that "nothing here carries attestation weight". But the whole progression record is derived live from an unbounded table: src/lib/db/migrations/011_drop_game_tables.sql:5 records that "level / streak / achievements is derived live from real activity", and src/lib/analytics/analytics-repository.ts computes lifetime facts with no time bound — distinctActiveDays() at :148 runs `SELECT DISTINCT date(created_at) FROM analytics_events ORDER BY d` over the entire table, and :286 runs `SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT event_type) FROM analytics_events`. src/lib/stats/derive.ts:22 confirms the inputs are "interaction-event-derived (analytics_events)". WG-ARCH-008's conflict demands exactly this table get "a prune, a TTL" it currently lacks. Add one and the operator's level drops and earned achievements un-earn retroactively — against ADR-0004's stated purpose: "the accumulated investment in a Body is real, currently invisible, and worth showing", and its decision 2, "Progression is per-Body... Each agent profile carries its own record." A record that shrinks when the log is pruned is a point-in-time fact being served from a cache, which is the one thing WG-ARCH-003's decision rule forbids ("Never store a derived value that is neither snapshot nor owned cache" — here it is neither, it is recomputed from erasable inputs).
findings.fix: Rule the collision explicitly rather than leaving it to whoever writes the first prune. Either (a) name analytics_events as retention-exempt in WG-ARCH-008's retention plan and say why, accepting unbounded growth on a machine meant to run for years, or (b) take WG-ARCH-003's C for the per-Body progression record — an immutable per-profile snapshot with its inputs digest, written before the first prune ships, with analytics_events then free to age out. (b) is what ADR-0004 decision 2 actually describes.

findings.problem: WG-WEB-001 is marked argued and grants a "scoped D exception" whose enabling condition the same ruling records as unmet. It blesses and condemns the same artefact in one entry, and the artefact it blesses breaches ADR-0003.
findings.evidence: WG-WEB-001-surface-register.md, on option D: "Consider D when long reads dominate and the print siblings are light, and the team accepts the second register's QC cost." The walk's own conflict says the opposite of that last clause: the rec-room reader "is an undeclared mixed register (option D) shipping inside a module, carrying a second QC surface nobody budgeted for". Verified at src/modules/rec-room/components/ReaderSettings.tsx:11 (`pageTheme: "dark" | "black" | "sepia" | "light"`), :33 sepia { bg #1c1812 } and :34 light { bg #f5f0e8, text #2c2c2c, accent #7c3aed } — raw hexes outside the token system, including a purple accent that exists in neither globals.css's ramp nor the kit. ADR-0003: "PatterStage stops minting design tokens immediately." And the kit has no light ground to vendor: PatterStudio/shared/ui/src/theme.css declares --color-void #05080d and --color-surface #0b121b only. So the exception cannot be sourced from the mandated kit and cannot be minted locally. Also note long reads do not dominate here — the walk itself rules 27 of 27 routes app shell in WG-WEB-002, which is D's other trigger failing.
findings.fix: Either delete the light and sepia page themes, which makes the A ruling true as stated and removes a QC surface and an ADR-0003 breach in one change; or fork it: "does the Story Weaver reader keep a light register, and who pays its QC?" What cannot stand is an argued ruling that grants an exception on a budget acceptance the same paragraph says was never given.

findings.problem: WG-DEL-002 is marked argued and puts a named journey in the trunk-blocking set whose content is undecided — WG-OPS-002, ruled later, forks on which install path a stranger even gets. An acceptance journey cannot be written for a deployment model that is still an open owner question.
findings.evidence: WG-DEL-002's ruling: "the full end-to-end acceptance suite, including the install journey, blocks main", and its conflict names the journey "guarding the venture's number-one cheapest death" as tests/integration/test_full_install_update_process.py. WG-OPS-002's FORK: "Does a stranger installing PatterStage get a third deployment model, and if so which?" with three costed options (install.sh only / promote the container / build the .exe). The journey differs completely across them, and option 2 is recorded as unable to run update or rebuild at all because .dockerignore excludes .git. Verified that today's path is scripts/bootstrap/install.sh:258, `git clone --branch "$BRANCH" --single-branch`, followed by scripts/bootstrap/setup.sh:211 `npm run build` — a journey that cannot run in CI unchanged, since it builds from network on a clean machine (see F3).
findings.fix: Split WG-DEL-002's ruling: B for the application acceptance journeys, which are determined and can be written now, and mark the install-journey clause needsOwner, blocked on the WG-OPS-002 fork. Or resolve WG-OPS-002 first and re-order devops ahead of delivery for this edge. Recording it as argued implies a journey is writable this week that is not.

findings.problem: WG-WEB-012 (A, generated only) and WG-DEL-003 (B, committed pixel baselines) collide on the exact cost WG-WEB-012 was ruled to protect, and neither names the other. Both are in the same walk; WG-WEB-012 is argued, WG-DEL-003 is forked on timing but not on the weight.
findings.evidence: WG-WEB-012's stated reason for A: "the asset-weight trigger bites harder here than on a hosted site: PatterStage ships as a clone or an .exe, so every megabyte is paid at install, not at page view", and its conflict warns that "a contributor could add a public/ directory of screenshots with a fully green build". WG-DEL-003's B mandates precisely that: "baselines committed and re-baselining a reviewed event" over "every kit component's states" — 25 files in src/components/ui — and re-baselining events accrete in history rather than replacing it. The install path takes the full history of the branch: scripts/bootstrap/install.sh:258 is `git clone --branch "$BRANCH" --single-branch "$REPO_URL"` with no --depth. .git is 29M today, so a committed PNG baseline set plus its re-baselines is a material multiple of the current clone cost on the surface that carries cheapest death #1.
findings.fix: Rule the interaction rather than leaving it to the first VRT commit. Options that keep both rulings: keep baselines out of the installed clone (a separate baselines branch or artefact store fetched only by CI), or accept the weight and shallow-clone the installer (`git clone --depth 1`), which costs nothing and caps history at one commit. Whichever, the media rule WG-WEB-012 asks design-lint to grow needs an explicit carve-out for the VRT baseline directory, or the two gates will fight.

findings.problem: WG-OPS-004 is marked argued and layers C (hard caps) on unattended agent work, but C's enabling clause is empty under the hosting ruling, so the ruling silently converts a platform setting into an unbudgeted product feature. There is also a genuine ordering cycle between the two wargames that the walk broke in the direction that let this through.
findings.evidence: WG-OPS-004-cost-ceilings.md decision rule: "Experiments, scratch estates and anything an unattended fleet can scale: C where the platform offers it, on top of B." WG-OPS-001 ruled C, self-hosting, and its own conflict states "PatterStage's runtime cost and pager transfer wholesale to the user, so there is no account, no region, no root holder" — there is no platform to offer a ceiling. A hard cap on a stranger's unattended agent loop therefore has to be built into the product, on a sole dev whose death #2 is "a sole dev's budget goes to connectors". The cycle: WG-OPS-001's decision rule names WG-OPS-004 as input ("No such trigger: A, spend-guarded by WG-OPS-004"), while WG-OPS-004's C clause depends on the hosting answer; the walk ruled 004 before 001, which is defensible but means the C layer was ruled before the fact that empties it was established. The walk names the deeper gap itself — "the wargame's 'whose money is it' axis has no row for a user you have never met" — and then rules argued anyway.
findings.fix: Split the ruling by whose money it is. B for the operator's own install is determined and cheap (a monthly figure, spend logged, triage pause). The stranger-facing hard cap is a product-scope decision with a build cost and no platform to inherit it from, so it is a fork: does PatterStage ship a spend ceiling for users, or does it ship a documented instruction to set one at the provider and a visible running total? Note the mitigating fact the ruling already found — llm-endpoint.ts supports local OpenAI-compatible providers, so a genuine zero-spend configuration exists — which is what makes this a choice rather than an obligation.
